definition: Redundancy means needless repetition or duplication.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word redundancy. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know redundancy should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The twins' chore board lists 'feed the dog' under both names — a redundancy the dog exploits nightly for second dinners.
A restatement repeats on purpose — to clarify or drive a point home; redundancy is the repeat that earns nothing.
Padding sits past redundancy on the editor's frown scale: not just the same thing twice, but bulk shoveled in purely to lengthen.

Duplication is a second copy of something that already exists — and it can even be deliberate: the backup file, the spare form in the drawer. Redundancy is duplication judged and found useless, the repeat that serves no purpose. Every redundancy contains a duplicate; only the pointless duplicate earns the name redundancy.

Wordiness wraps a real point in more words than it needs — the message survives, buried under throat-clearing and ornament. Redundancy is a different flaw: the point is made, then made again for free. Wordy writing says one thing slowly; redundancy says the same thing twice.

English legal writing is famous for its paired phrases: contracts are declared 'null and void,' warnings demand that someone 'cease and desist,' property passes 'free and clear.' The pairs began as translation insurance.
After 1066, English courts served speakers of English and speakers of French, so lawyers wrote key terms twice -- once in each language -- to be understood by both.
Nine centuries later the two languages have merged, and in each pair both words now mean exactly the same thing.
What survives is pure redundancy: the second word of each pair adds no meaning a court would ever weigh.
Style guides urge lawyers to cut the doubled terms, and tradition, so far, keeps winning.
